introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2024. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 5 c) : les industries du Nord (égrenage et huilerie du coton autour de Garoua, Maroua et Guider ; riz de la SEMRY à Yagoua et Maga ; cimenterie de Figuil ; brasserie de Garoua ; barrage de Lagdo) sont citées de mémoire comme exemples reconnus ; la liste exacte des usines, leurs localisations et le détail des usines textiles ne sont pas certains et sont énoncés en termes généraux. Le sujet écrit « Northern Lowlands » ; le corrigé l'interprète comme les plaines de la Bénoué et de l'Extrême-Nord. À faire relire par un géographe.
Question 5 b) : la ligne de chemin de fer citée (Bélabo - Yaoundé - Douala) est le réseau de l'axe est-ouest .

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur donnés avec « about » ou « more than ». Les faits cités sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3, Section B : questions 4 à 6, Section C : question 7 seule). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 offre deux versions (EITHER / OR) de trois sous-questions : codées « a », « b », « c » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b », « OR-c » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou`.

Sujet scanné de cinq pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions, une page de planche de carte topographique 1:50 000 « Dufftown » avec ses signes conventionnels, puis le fond de carte du Cameroun pour la question 3c i). Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2024, Three Hours. Filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés. La planche topographique (page 4) appartient aux épreuves de cartographie (Paper 3) et ne sert à aucune question de ce Paper 2 : non transcrite. Seul le fond de carte du Cameroun (page 5) est utilisé (question 3).

Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment bien à 25 (Q1 8+8+9, Q2 6+10+9, Q3 8+8+(3+6=9), Q4 6+10+9, Q5 5+9+11, Q6 8+9+8, Q7 EITHER 9+8+8, OR 6+10+9). Aucun écart avec le sujet. Le sujet imprime des marks pour un ensemble de sous-points (ex. Q1 a (i)+(ii) = 8 marks) : le corrigé les regroupe sous une seule sous-question.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) How would a farmer maximise the use of his land where there is land scarcity?

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Where land is scarce, the farmer cannot extend the farmed area, so he must raise the **output from each hectare**, that is, farm more **intensively**, by the following methods (about 1 mark each, with examples).

1. **Mixed cropping and intercropping**: growing two or more crops on the same plot at the same time (maize with beans and cocoyams, vegetables beneath banana trees), and **multiple cropping** (two or three crops each year) so that the land is never idle.
2. **Shorter fallows and crop rotation**, with the use of **manure, compost and chemical fertilisers**, to maintain soil fertility without leaving land fallow; improved seeds and early-maturing, high-yielding varieties.
3. **Terracing, ridges and raised beds** to farm steep slopes and wet valley floors (as in the Bamenda and Bamileke highlands and in Rwanda, Nepal or the Philippines), and **irrigation** or **market gardening** (including dry-season gardening along streams) so that crops can grow all year.
4. **Intensive livestock and aquaculture on small areas**: stall-feeding (zero grazing) of cattle, goats or pigs, poultry houses, rabbits, fish ponds; the manure is returned to the crops.
5. **Agroforestry and the use of every space**: trees and crops together (e.g. cocoa and plantain, or fodder trees), kitchen gardens around the house, vertical or greenhouse farming, and the reclamation of swamps and marginal land; **cooperative** farming and consolidation of plots can also raise yields.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Discuss **THREE** reasons why an economic operator dealing with timber would prefer railway over road transport.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Timber (logs and sawn wood) is **bulky, heavy and of low value per tonne**, and it is moved over long distances from the forest to the sawmill and then to the port (in Cameroon, from the East and South regions to the port of Douala). Railways have several advantages for such cargo (3 marks each).

**1. Lower cost per tonne over long distances, and large carrying capacity.** One train, with many wagons, carries as much timber as dozens of lorries, with lower fuel and labour costs per tonne-kilometre, so that, for the long haul to the port, the unit cost is lower and the profit margin higher. Long logs of great weight can be carried on flat wagons with fewer loading restrictions. (Road transport is cheaper for short distances and for the first stage from the forest to the railhead, so the combination of a lorry to the station and a train to the port is often used, for example to the railway line from Bélabo to Yaoundé and Douala.)

**2. Reliability and less risk of delay and damage.** Trains run on a timetable on a dedicated track, are less affected by heavy rain than the earth roads of the forest (which often become impassable in the wet season) and are less exposed to traffic jams, roadblocks and breakdowns, so the operator can meet export deadlines and ship schedules; there is less damage and loss of timber, and less theft in transit than on the road with many stops.

**3. Safety, legal and environmental advantages.** Overloaded log lorries damage roads and are involved in many road accidents; the lorry operator faces axle-load limits, fines, and the cost of repairs and tyres, while rail transport is safer and avoids the problem. The railway uses less fuel per tonne and produces less carbon dioxide, which helps the company's image and compliance with timber certification.

**Limits (for balance):** the railway is **inflexible** (fixed routes and times), it needs loading and unloading (transfer) at stations and a road for the first and last stages, and the railway network is limited and the capacity of wagons may not meet the demand, so many operators still use road transport. On the whole, for long distances and large volumes, rail is preferred.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Explain how the major industries in the Northern Lowlands of Cameroon are linked to their sources of raw materials.

(11 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Northern Lowlands** (the Benue plains and the lowlands of the Far North: the Garoua, Maroua and Yagoua areas) have a tropical continental (Sudan) climate with a short rainy season. Their economy is based on the cultivation of **cotton, rice, sorghum and millet**, groundnuts and livestock rearing, and the main industries are **agro-processing and a few mineral-based industries**, located near to the raw materials because these raw materials are bulky and lose weight in processing, which would make transport to a distant factory costly. The main links are as follows.

**1. Cotton: ginning, cotton-seed oil, soap and textiles.** Cotton is the main cash crop of the North and Far North, grown by small farmers under the supervision and support (inputs, credit, purchase) of the cotton company **SODECOTON**. **Ginneries** are located in the cotton-growing areas, in towns such as Garoua, Maroua and Guider and other centres, since the seed cotton loses about two-thirds of its weight on ginning (the lint is separated from the seed). The cotton seed is the raw material for **oil mills and soap-making**, and the cotton fibre supplies **textile** mills, which are in the same region or in the south (such as the Douala textile works).

**2. Rice: rice milling.** Rice is grown on irrigated rice schemes of the Logone and Chari floodplain in the Far North (the SEMRY project around **Yagoua and Maga**), and the paddy is processed in **rice mills** located at the schemes. The mills are near to the raw material, which is bulky and perishable, and the by-products (husk and bran) are used for animal feed.

**3. Livestock: meat, hides and skins, leather and dairy products.** The North and Far North have most of the cattle, sheep and goats of the country (the Fulani and Shuwa Arab herders), and the abattoirs, cold stores, tanneries and leather workshops in **Garoua and Maroua** use the animals and the hides. Some meat is sent by road and by rail from Ngaoundere to the south and exported to the neighbouring countries.

**4. Limestone: cement.** The cement works at **Figuil** (the Benue valley) are located on the **limestone** deposits that supply the main raw material; limestone is very bulky and heavy and a large quantity is used per tonne of cement, so the cement plant is placed at the quarry (a weight-losing industry) and the cement is sent to the northern markets and neighbouring Chad and Nigeria.

**5. Other industries linked to local materials:** the brewery and drink industry of Garoua, which uses the water of the Benue and local cereals; fish processing and drying, which relies on the fish of the Lagdo reservoir, the Benue and the Lake Chad area; and the small workshops that use local materials (pottery, leather goods, metal work, weaving).

**Factors reinforcing the link:** the raw material comes from the region and the cost of transporting the goods is high (long distance to the south, poor roads, and the railway ends at Ngaoundere, so the rail link to Douala is far to the south); the **Lagdo hydro-electric dam** on the Benue provides power; and there is a large labour supply and the markets of Nigeria and Chad.

**Conclusion:** the industries of the Northern Lowlands are mostly **primary processing** of local farm and mineral products, located close to the source of their materials; the region exports these and has few manufacturing industries that depend on imported materials.
